title: Walking in the city
hook: the walk to the bus can be meditation too

segments.voice: Yesterday, samadhi, the five blessings of walking: stamina, strength for effort, health, good digestion, and a concentration that lasts. Your line was walking steadies. Did you take a slow walk after a meal? Day one hundred twenty-one.

This week you've had a lane. Fifteen quiet steps, a slow turn, fifteen back. Lovely. Now picture Tuesday at 8:12. You're late, the coffee is too hot, the bus is two blocks away and pulling in. Nobody on that sidewalk is lifting, moving and placing. There's a horn, a dog, a man on a speakerphone. It's easy to think meditation lives in the lane and the city is where it goes to die. Today's question is simple: does the walk to the bus count too? The old texts have an answer, and it's a generous one.
screen: `FIFTEEN QUIET STEPS.` → `TUESDAY, 8:12, THE BUS.` → `DOES THIS WALK COUNT?`

segments.voice: The lane is a training ground, not the whole game. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Buddha describes a practitioner who knows the body in every posture. When walking, they know they're walking. When standing, they know they're standing. Sitting, lying down: the same. The text then goes further. Going out and coming back, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, eating, drinking, even using the toilet: all of it can be done with clear knowing. The word for that is sampajanna, clear comprehension. It means you know what you're doing while you're doing it, and why. Nothing in that list requires a quiet lane. So a city walk is a real practice, just a different one. In the lane you slow everything down. On the sidewalk you walk at a normal pace, eyes open, watching for traffic, because clear knowing includes knowing the curb is there. What you bring is the thread: the feel of the feet. Heel, sole, toes, the next foot. When the mind jumps to the meeting, the text message, the argument you're rehearsing, you notice it and come back to the feet. Some teachers use the city itself as the bell. Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen teacher, suggested treating a red light or a ringing phone as a small call home to the breath. You're stopped anyway; you might as well arrive. So the walk to the bus isn't wasted time between practice sessions. For someone with a job and kids and a commute, it may be most of the practice there's time for. The feet are always with you.
screen: `THE LANE IS TRAINING, NOT THE GAME.` · `WALKING, KNOW YOU'RE WALKING.` · `NORMAL PACE, EYES OPEN, FEET FIRST.` · `A RED LIGHT AS A BELL.` · then, large: `EVERY STEP, HERE.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can, wherever you are. Feel the floor under both feet. Now walk a few steps at your ordinary speed, the speed you'd walk to the bus, not the slow lane speed. Feel each foot land: heel, sole, toes. Stop. Stand. Let the breath come and go. Then sit, and for the rest of this time, picture tomorrow's first real walk: the door, the street, the corner. Pick one spot on that route, a crosswalk or a stoplight, that will be your bell. The bell holds the time.
Sampajanna. Clear comprehension, knowing what you're doing while you do it: walking in the city, at a normal pace, eyes open, the feet as the thread.

Your line: every step, here. Today, on one real walk, even thirty seconds to the car or the mailbox, feel your feet the whole way. When you reach your chosen spot, arrive there. Day one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers encourage walking practice outside the retreat lane: on the way to work, in a parking lot, at a stoplight, simply knowing the body is walking while walking at a normal pace.

match.prompt: match the piece to what it means on a city walk.
pairs: a training ground, slow and quiet
clear knowing: what you're doing, and why
the thread you come back to
a bell the city rings for you

myth: walking meditation only counts if you walk very slowly
in the city you walk at a normal pace; the practice is knowing you're walking.
the old text lists eating, drinking and even the toilet as times for clear knowing
the discourse on mindfulness includes all of those, not just the meditation hall.
mindful walking means closing your eyes to go inward
eyes stay open: clear knowing includes knowing where the curb is.

fork.setup: you're on the sidewalk, rehearsing an argument with your boss. you notice. what now?
options: stop walking until the thought is gone.
notice it, and come back to the feet.
give up: the city is too loud to practice.
fork.reveal: that's the whole practice: notice where the mind went, and return to the feel of the feet. you keep walking the whole time.

original.note: Pali: clear comprehension, knowing what you're doing while you do it; paired with sati, mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation needs a quiet room, and the city is noise.
what it means: every posture counts; walking to the bus, knowing you're walking, is practice.
what a scholar hears: the satipatthana discourse lists the four postures and then daily acts like eating and dressing under sampajanna, clear comprehension.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta), the postures and clear comprehension
Thich Nhat Hanh, teaching on red lights and ringing phones as bells of mindfulness

notes: The postures and the list of daily acts under clear comprehension are paraphrased from MN 10 / DN 22; confirm the list (going forward and back, looking ahead and away, bending and stretching, eating, drinking, urinating and defecating).
Thich Nhat Hanh is named and paraphrased (red lights and telephone rings as bells of mindfulness); not quoted.
Practice sized to a two-minute sit: a few ordinary-speed steps, then sitting and choosing a 'bell' on tomorrow's route.
